items.title: Three small failures combined to take down Microsoft 365
items.excerpt: A hidden defect in Microsoft's cloud gateway, dormant since July, was to blame for one of the largest outages in the company's history last week. A preliminary Post-Incident Report (PIR) released by the company outlines how the latent bug, changes in traffic, and reduced server capacity combined to knock much of Microsoft 365 and Exchange infrastructure offline at the end of last week. Microsoft's report lists the incident's final status as "a technical issue not related to cyber or AI/agents." Microsoft's preliminary report places the outage between November 12 at 16:20 UTC and November 13 at 16:10 UTC, just under 24 hours total, and additional monitoring remained in place for any affected systems through November 14. The outage started on November 12 and quickly rippled through businesses and public offices that depend on Microsoft's cloud and email exchange infrastructure. The outage is covered in Microsoft's incident IDs EX1550543 and MO1550821. You need Microsoft 365 admin credentials to see the full report on the company's status pages, but Office Watch has reproduced the preliminary report , and the University of Pennsylvania maintains an archive of Microsoft's service-health updates . items.title: Hyperscale data centers use 2% of US electricity
items.excerpt: One flashpoint for the tech industry’s all-in push on large language models has been the sudden rush to turn investment money into hyperscale data centers. The rush hasn’t allowed anyone to plan how to supply the required electricity cleanly or with minimal impact on ratepayers. Instead, it has been difficult to even collect information on what’s being built. A new study has tallied energy use and estimated emissions for hyperscalers operating in the United States between May 2024 and April 2025. They weren’t able to differentiate between AI compute and more traditional data services, but it provides a clear point of reference to track moving forward. Finding the centers The team started with a list of 675 facilities from a commercial database based on news reports, company statements, and satellite imagery. They dropped any that didn’t have a reported electrical capacity or that they couldn’t verify was a suitably large building with the expected cooling and electrical connection equipment. That reduced the list to 403 data centers with an average electrical capacity of about 40 megawatts. Read full article Comments

They stream tokens, call tools mid-response, update shared state, pause for a human, and spawn subagents, and every framework does it differently. items.title: My AI Agents Write Code Faster Than I Can Verify It
items.excerpt: 76% of developers and engineering managers in Sonar's 2027 State of Code report say they generate AI code faster than they can verify it! And I'm right there with them, since I run software factories where agents open pull requests around the clock. AI code looks correct way more often now, so the bugs that slip through are the subtle ones. The way I handle it in my own factories is simple. Agents can write whatever they want, but nothing merges until a check the agent doesn't control says it passes. The full report is really worth a read if you're handing more of your code to agents: https://fandf.co/4iN1mvB Thanks to Sonar for working with me on this!

Safe, controlled releases with guardrails. Check out Release Autopilot: https://fandf.co/4sttJ6l Thanks to LaunchDarkly for working with me on this! #ad

items.title: Your Coding Agent Has a MASSIVE Blind Spot (You Need to Fix It)
items.excerpt: I've had agents break hundreds of times in production (sometimes in very embarrassing ways), and almost all the time it comes down to the blind spots in my coding agent. Your agent sees your code, but not what it does once it's running. The Dynatrace MCP Server brings live production data to the coding agent in your IDE, so you can ask about your running systems in plain language and trace a problem to the exact line behind it. items.title: Learning by doing: Moore's law, Wright's law, Arrow's law
items.excerpt: Economists studying technological progress contrast invention to learning by doing. Invention is doing something new, whereas learning by doing is doing the same thing over and over. One example of invention is LED lighting. Ravers with LEDs of course look futuristic, but now that LED lighting is widespread, the whole world looks a little different, and old indoor photos look old just because of the quality of the light. It was a total trend break from the steady improvement of incandescent lighting since Edison. LED lighting required a new material: gallium nitride for the blue LED. My postdoc work was in materials discovery, and blue LEDs and lithium-ion batteries were aspirational examples. Solar power, though, was an uncomfortable reminder of how much technological progress had nothing to do with us. The solar boom was not because of academics working on exciting alternatives to silicon in the lab, but decades of accumulated progress in manufacturing with silicon. (The exception is America's only major solar cell manufacturer, First Solar; they use cadmium telluride.) I first saw a graph like this at a conference: On the y axis is log price, and on the x axis is log cumulative production: that is, how many solar panels have ever been made, measured in watts. When we see a line on a graph like this, we call it an instance of "Wright's Law". Soon enough I saw these graphs everywhere online; this one is from OWID . items.title: Safety Cases Have an Agent Foundations Problem
items.excerpt: If we want to ensure that AI systems are safe, should we approach the problem like an engineer, or a scientist? Do we need to discover deep and fundamental truths about how intelligence works, or is it better to focus our efforts on applying the battle-tested methods developed by safety engineers over the course of decades? As others have noted , this question is beginning to become a crux of disagreement between those who are concerned about the risks posed by advanced AI systems, and those who are relatively confident that humanity will muddle through. In this post I argue that it isn't clear how to use these safety engineering methods, or whether they work for advanced AI systems, because you immediately run into thorny scientific problems when you try to apply them. Furthermore, these thorny scientific problems are the same ones being studied under the banner of Agent Foundations. I'll start by laying out my understanding of how safety assurance typically works. Here, I'm drawing from what I've learnt as a PhD student embedded in the University of York's safety assurance research community. Then, I'll try to apply that framework to a highly capable AI system, and discuss some problems that come up. How Does Safety Assurance Work? It has nevertheless been historically very strange for me to see how closely associated "AI doomers" and short timelines have been in the popular imagination. As anybody who's interacted with the AI risk case will realize, timelines are (at least in theory) mostly orthogonal with your beliefs on AI safety. Yes, timelines have some impact on what kinds of interventions are going to be viable, but among people who "believe in AGI" the variance in their optimism about the problem is more immediately dependent on underlying technical questions than anything else. Before GPT-2 or AlphaGo, there was still a much smaller, nascent "AI safety community", and these people were certainly not basing their worries on some data about AI uplift that we only got in 2026. However, for years people on general social media have taken it on faith that the "AI safety position" and "short timelines position" were the same, and even argued against short timelines as if in doing so they were arguing against "doomers." items.title: AI Company Employees Should Unionize
items.excerpt: I. Should safety-conscious employees at AI companies quit in protest, or stay and fight? The latest argument didn’t resolve the dispute, but it did get me in contact with organizers working on both sides. Those planning to stay and fight are increasingly interested in labor organization. This doesn’t need to mean literal government-recognized Labor Unions. An existing group, Coalition Of Concerned AI Staff , is already helping support interested employees and investigating other models to do more. But it might involve using laws, rights, and tactics associated with the National Labor Relations Act and the labor movement. You may remember stories of bitter unionization battles at places like Starbucks, but AI workers can probably route around that. The toughest labor disputes happen in fields where the employer could easily fire all the organized workers and replace them from a bottomless pool of faceless scabs: although this is illegal, everyone needs to be maximally lawyered-up to prevent it. But there are so few skilled AI researchers that these laws are hardly necessary; if a dozen top AI researchers threaten to walk, it doesn’t matter whether Section P Sub-Section Q forces the AI company to negotiate - the AI company will want to negotiate. items.title: Escaping The “Outside Criticism” Trap
items.excerpt: I. Here’s a fun argument you can use to discredit anyone at any time. Start by calling them an arrogant fanatic with a totalizing ideology, someone who thinks they personally have solved all problems and can’t possibly learn from anyone who disagrees. If they have friends who agree with them, they’re a cult who collectively work to shelter themselves from any dissenting viewpoint. Then your victim responds by presenting one hundred notarized affadavits describing times when they have engaged with their critics, spent years studying books by their critics to see what they could learn from them, and even changed their beliefs in response to criticism. Then you spring the trap: “Ah, but you cherry-picked critics who operate within your worldview, a sort of loyal opposition. You continue to dismiss and exclude genuine critics who challenge your smug assumptions.” This always works. If your victim protests that they do like and appreciate many critics with worldviews different to theirs, you object that no, those guys are also within the system. items.title: When Should LLM Agents Forget? Memory Filtering Under Query-Critical Resolver Errors
items.excerpt: arXiv:2611.17338v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM memory systems often delete facts classified as stale. We show that this hard-filtering step can reduce downstream accuracy when resolver errors delete query-critical facts. Across three models, a controlled sensitivity intervention moves hard-drop from gains of +0.186 to +0.230 at perfect resolution to losses of -0.176 to -0.181 at the lowest tested reliability. Paired targeted interventions show that false-drop causes significantly greater degradation than false-keep, while a non-deleting baseline can still fail when incorrect labels steer generation. On a frozen 102/102 calibration/test split, a simple deployment-matched gate reaches 0.655 accuracy versus 0.641 for always hard-drop and 0.662 for test-informed oracle selection. Global-accuracy crossovers require gold labels and are model- and task-specific diagnostics, not deployment thresholds. Deletion should instead be treated as cost-sensitive: validate query-critical false-drop risk on matched data, or default to label-free retention when such validation is unavailable.

items.title: Does the Ranking Hold? A Practitioner-Facing Audit of Hallucination Detectors on Small, Quantized, On-Device LLMs
items.excerpt: arXiv:2611.17339v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hallucination detection for large language models is dominated by methods evaluated on 7B-70B research models with abundant sampling budgets and exact-match or ROUGE correctness labels. The small models practitioners actually ship on-device, Phi-3-mini, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-2B-Instruct, typically at 4-bit precision, sit outside this evidence base. We present a reproducible one-GPU audit of four detectors spanning three paradigms: length-normalized token-margin calibration, a lexical n-gram baseline, and two sampling-based consistency methods (semantic entropy and SelfCheckGPT-NLI) on two small open instruction-tuned models (Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct) loaded at 4-bit NF4 quantization on a single Colab T4 GPU, evaluated on closed-book TriviaQA. Cross-model ranking transfer is poor: Spearman rho is -0.80 and Kendall tau-b is -0.667, meaning the detector ranking actively inverts between the two models, and the cheap lexical baseline is statistically indistinguishable from the sampling-based consistency detectors on both models under bootstrap 95 percent confidence intervals. As a second, methodological contribution, we show that the standard token-overlap-to-multiple-choice correctness labeler for TruthfulQA-Generation produces near-chance AUROC (0.46-0.59) for all four detectors on both models, a labeler failure, not a detector failure, since the same detectors reach 0.69-0.89…

items.title: LoRAWeaver: Directional Adapter Routing in LoRA Representation Space
items.excerpt: arXiv:2611.17340v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models are expensive to update through full retraining. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning reduces the cost of adaptation, but repeated adaptation creates a growing pool of task-specific LoRA adapters. This pool complicates adapter selection during inference. Existing routing and encoder-based methods often require retraining when new adapters are added, which limits their use in dynamic settings. This paper treats adapter routing as a representation alignment problem in the adapter-output space. The proposed training-free method selects adapters by matching adapter-conditioned query representations against task prototypes using cosine similarity. Experiments with LLaMA-2-7B and LLaMA-2-13B on a 48-task FLAN-v2 benchmark and on out-of-distribution tasks show that the method outperforms training-free baselines in the cross-task setting and approaches a trained retrieval encoder without learning a router. An ablation confirms the benefit of directional alignment in the adapter-output space.

items.title: Tabular Population Priors as Structured Retrieval for EHR Medication Set Prediction
items.excerpt: arXiv:2611.17341v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Medication prediction from electronic health records is a fixed vocabulary structured prediction problem, yet recent clinical RAG systems often treat it like open ended case based reasoning: retrieve similar patient admissions and ask an LLM to infer a medication set. This retrieval object is indirect the model receives retrieved patient records while the target is a discrete set of medication class labels. We propose a more task aligned retrieval object: a tabular population prior ranked medication class candidates from a sparse condition medication co occurrence table estimated from training admissions. Using PACERAG as a fixed downstream pipeline and replacing only its patient retriever, this drop in swap improves F1 from 0.303 to 0.338 (+11.5% relative) and Jaccard from 0.218 to 0.237 on 1,004 heldout MIMIC IV admissions, with no additional LLM calls and no inference time patient index. A non LLM top k baseline reaches F1=0.248, confirming the prior is predictive before LLM integration. Aggregate population statistics can provide a more task aligned, efficient, and auditable retrieval source than patient level nearest neighbors for fixed vocabulary EHR set prediction.

items.title: An Operationalization of Opaque Serial Depth
items.excerpt: arXiv:2611.17495v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) is currently a valuable tool for overseeing AI models, but some architectural shifts could significantly reduce CoT monitorability. We operationalize a measure that serves as a proxy for the amount of unverbalized serial cognition a model can perform, as a specific instantiation of the notion of opaque serial depth: roughly, the length of the longest path through a model's computation that does not pass through an interpretable bottleneck. Our main contribution is a particular standard for what counts as such a bottleneck. We define natural-language-rooted (NL-rooted) nodes as nodes that were initialized from a pre-training prior to produce human-understandable outputs, whose output space has not been expanded beyond that prior, and whose outputs the model has not been modified to interpret as a different type of data. By construction, the resulting measure, NLS depth, can be adjudicated before training from an architecture, training recipe, and deployment configuration alone, and is insensitive to ordinary post-training such as prompting, distillation, and RL. We find that, across open-weight models, NLS depth correlates strongly with layer count, with some exceptions, and has grown slowly over recent years. items.title: Build once, run on any agent: A practical guide to agent skills
items.excerpt: How many times this week did you re-explain the same task to an agent? How many times did you ask your colleague with deep institutional knowledge how to solve a specific problem? That context shouldn’t be lost in a chat or locked in one person’s head. Agent skills let you capture repeatable instructions so you and your agents can reuse them. The skill you write for yourself tonight can later become part of a team’s pipeline. An agent skill is a versioned directory centered on a SKILL.md file that describes when and how to do a repeatable task. You can share those instructions across agents, but the environment still needs to provide the tools, credentials, and permissions to carry them out. A skill can describe how to query a database, for example, but it doesn’t grant access to that database. I covered this topic live with Shishir Tewari, Senior Manager, Data Engineering at Procore, during GitHub Universe 2026. Our session was titled “Build once, run on any agent: a practical guide to agent skills” . Define one job and when it applies A skill works best when it has a clear job, input, and output. For example, let’s say you’re building an agent that checks AI-generated changes against the original request. If the same agent assesses its own work, its explanation might influence the review. These include arbitrary code execution when recursively cloning a malicious repository, writes to unintended files, and memory corruption when processing merges or binary patches. We recommend updating to Git 2.56.1 or the patched release for your maintenance series, and updating any applications that bundle Git. Vulnerabilities in Git CVE-2026-111760: Code execution during recursive clones Git checks paths before writing files into a working tree, including rejecting paths that would overwrite its own repository metadata. items.title: Inside GitHub’s new Git storage architecture
items.excerpt: Last week at GitHub Universe, we announced our new Git storage architecture, capable of handling thousands of writes per second with reads that scale on demand. Through internal testing, we’ve demonstrated the ability to support 5,000 concurrent agents working on a repository, sending 7,200 pushes per second to a repo, all while serving read traffic with consistently low latency. This new architecture is the foundation for GitHub to support agentic development for hundreds of millions of developers, and we’ve been building it underneath GitHub while it keeps running. Over the past year, agents changed what a busy repository looks like on GitHub. In our first post in this series, we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation Git storage architecture: minimize coordination, and decouple storage from compute. In our last post , we covered the bridge: moving 99.99999% of repositories into Azure, scoping the write quorum to individual references, and standing up virtual replicas backed by Azure Blob Storage. We also left off with an observation: very little of a write needs to be ordered. Git objects are immutable and named by their contents, meaning two writers can store them at the same time without agreeing on anything. The part of a push that needs agreement is the reference update, and a reference update is tiny in comparison. items.excerpt: Of the many chemicals humans have invented to control agricultural pests, some of the most devious are called “ insect growth regulators .” As the name suggests, these compounds don’t kill insects directly; they alter their development so they can’t grow into healthy, reproducing adults. This makes insect growth regulators a remarkably useful tool for taming populations of insects like whiteflies and mealybugs, which can spread diseases and sap nutrients out of food crops. There’s just one problem: Farmers don’t want to regulate all insects in this way. Beneficial insects like honey bees risk getting caught in the crosshairs of these chemicals, to the detriment of farmers who need their pollination services to produce crops like pears and cherries. One insect growth regulator in particular has emerged as a potential issue for pollinators: buprofezin. Ongoing research out of Washington State University, or WSU, suggests that buprofezin may be hazardous to honey bees even at concentrations 10 times below those commonly found in pollen. A study published in 2024 connected the compound to “severe brood mortality.” At a meeting of the Washington State Beekeeping Association last month, WSU entomology professor Brandon Hopkins said buprofezin products should be sold with a pollinator warning — a break from current requirements of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, or EPA.
